name: Open Source Software

claims.claim_text: The only substantive difference between proprietary and open source software is that with open source you receive the code and may do with it whatever the licence allows; everything else commonly attached to either label is convention rather than consequence.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only difference between proprietary and open source software is like open source software, you get the code
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: A vendor compiler built on GCC must ship its source, which means the mechanism that disables optimisation in the free edition is visible in that source and can be compiled away; the paid version's difference is optimisation for speed and code size rather than function.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the source code is effectively the instructions on how to bypass that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bowie and The Brown Note

claims.claim_text: The peripheral libraries shipped alongside such a compiler are usually not open: they remain the vendor's copyright, cannot be redistributed, and carry a licence term restricting their use to that vendor's parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't take their library and go and compile it for an Atmel
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Bowie and The Brown Note

claims.claim_text: Charging only for the highest optimisation levels of an otherwise free toolchain works commercially because the customer is already locked to the silicon vendor and will pay the tax rather than change parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: if they put a paywall in place, you're just going to pay the tax and move on
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Engineering Optimization

claims.claim_text: The open-core pattern puts the widely wanted capability outside the open licence: a virtualisation package is open source while its USB support arrives as a proprietary extension.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want USB 2.0 support, you have to download a proprietary extension
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Kickstarter, Manufacturing, Open Hardware - Judging Jurisdictional Junctures

claims.claim_text: An author can be prevented from opening part of their own product by an agreement upstream: one popular board's libraries are open while its bootloader stays closed because the author signed a non-disclosure agreement with the silicon vendor.
claims.quote_verbatim: it uses a proprietary NDA bootloader
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Rubber Duck Incarnate

claims.claim_text: Licences described as open but conditioned on non-commercial use or on payment when money is made are a different arrangement from open source, and the distinction is worth stating plainly when describing a project.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm not saying like, oh, it's open, but you know, non-commercial and blah, blah, blah
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: A casual attitude to licence choice survives only while nothing is for sale; organisations with legal teams care which licence applies, which is when the choice starts to matter.
claims.quote_verbatim: These are companies and organizations and people with legal teams that care about this stuff
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Man Behind The Curtain

claims.claim_text: Publishing working code converts a gift into an obligation: users arrive wanting technical support, bug fixes and better documentation, and what began as a personal project becomes unpaid maintenance work.
claims.quote_verbatim: this little sort of gift to the world becomes this massive responsibility
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: Selling hardware whose software is written by volunteers creates a support mismatch the buyer does not perceive: the purchaser holds the hardware vendor responsible for defects in software that was given away and that the vendor did not write.
claims.quote_verbatim: the software is created by a community of volunteers and given away for free
claims.speaker: Chris Anderson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Chris Anderson - Deambulatory Daedal Drones

claims.claim_text: A common misreading is that free-to-use implies nobody spent time building it and nobody is spending time maintaining it, which sets the expectations that maintainers then have to manage.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of people think that if something is open source, it means it should be free
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Having published firmware and files under one's own name attracts approaches from prospective clients whose expectations of free work are unreasonable, which is a cost of visibility rather than a benefit of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the expectation of the people that were approaching me so far were just, uh, just crazy
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: Electronics Consultant Impedance Matching

claims.claim_text: Losing control of the code base is a real hazard of publishing: contributions that worked well at the outset can age badly and become the original author's problem to rewrite later.
claims.quote_verbatim: the danger of losing control of your code base
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: A single-maintainer project stalls on the maintainer's available time rather than on money or interest; because the source is published, anyone who wants the result badly enough can take it forward, and for some authors seeing the thing exist matters more than being the one who built it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they can still always take all the open source that I have posted and build their own version
claims.speaker: Jeff Roberg
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Rowberg - Mini Module Master

claims.claim_text: The bus-factor worry usually attaches to a lone open source maintainer, but the equivalent in the closed world is a supplier going out of business, after which the software and its source are simply gone; with open source the code survives and can be picked up, maintained or forked privately.
claims.quote_verbatim: the maintainer gets hit by a bus, but like someone can pick it up
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: A services company can be paid to build something and still push the result upstream, and the argument that persuades the paying customer is that they are already standing on a large amount of work contributed by others without paying for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're benefiting from a lot of work that has been done by other people without you having to pay for it
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Building in the open functions as evidence rather than marketing: prospective customers download the thing, try it, satisfy themselves that it is real, and arrive already convinced, which makes them the best customers to work with.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you just put things out there, if you show them, hey, I'm building this in the open, people will believe you much easier
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Fear of being copied is largely misplaced: competitors are busy pursuing their own aims, and publishing part of a system does not let anyone reconstruct how the whole connects. Companies typically start by opening a narrow area where doing so costs them nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: even if you open source half of your stuff, like nobody's going to be able to copy it easily
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Controlling the whole toolchain shortens the interval between finding a defect and fixing it, and that interval is what governs developer productivity; contributing directly to an open compiler avoids the overhead of coordinating a change with an outside company, however willing that company is.
claims.quote_verbatim: the time between, uh, finding a problem and fixing a problem, um, is really important to productivity
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: The compounding benefit is that a defect fixed once stays fixed for everyone, and the corresponding waste is rewriting the same peripheral controller repeatedly without a reason to.
claims.quote_verbatim: we shouldn't be writing yet another I squared C controller
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tim "Mithro" Ansell

claims.claim_text: Opening a hardware vendor's toolchain brings software engineers to devices they would otherwise never touch, producing improvements the vendor could not have made itself; it also reduces the vendor's own support burden of gluing separate proprietary tools together and explaining tools it does not fully understand.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can start seeing improvements take place in the community that you wouldn't do yourself
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Being able to compile the tools from source or take the vendor's binaries lets customers choose according to their own skills, which is a different proposition from a single vertical development environment.
claims.quote_verbatim: The fact that you can compile from source means that people can sort of, they have the flexibility depending on their skill set
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Industry consortia coordinate open cores and tools so that companies designing chips can see what they are building on; the effort spans synthesis tools, processor cores and the layers that tie them together.
claims.quote_verbatim: focusing on IP cores and software tools that are ideally open source
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: The standing criticism of the model is fragmentation: disagreement produces a fork rather than a resolution, leaving many versions of the same thing each carrying its own defects, and dividing scarce programming talent between them.
claims.quote_verbatim: you end up with 25 versions of essentially the same thing, each having their own unique problems
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: Flight controller firmware is the worked example of that pattern: an early simple controller was forked into a cleaner version, then again and again into separate projects, some rewritten entirely and each aimed at a particular use such as racing or autonomous navigation.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's probably four or five forks of the original code out there now
claims.speaker: Bruce Simson
claims.episode_title: Missle Man with Bruce Simson

claims.claim_text: Without an official binary a project cannot be supported: when a user reports a fault, nobody knows what they are running, because they compiled it themselves. A canonical build is a prerequisite for a support community rather than a compromise of principle.
claims.quote_verbatim: if there's no official or de facto standard, at least, executable, then how do you support this shit
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Firmware, Netburner and Semiconductors - Chris's Capitalism Colloquy

claims.claim_text: The same absence keeps professional users away: no central place to download a build, with executables on a contributor's personal site, reads as unserious to someone deciding whether to adopt a tool at work.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's no central repository for even downloading windows executables
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Motivational Speaker

claims.claim_text: A narrow field can support only one dominant open project, because the people who can write the code, want to work on tools, and understand the domain are a small intersection; that is why an early competitor to a now-dominant design tool faded rather than coexisting with it.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's probably a pretty small group of people that are like, like that group of developers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Data Provenance in the Home, Server, and Fab

claims.claim_text: Comparing project velocities across domains is misleading: a graphics tool with a very large user base, commercial users and substantial monthly donations funds a full-time staff, and expecting a niche design tool with a fraction of that base to move at the same pace mistakes scale for competence.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the bad things about Blender is it set an unrealistic standard for open source software
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LEDs Everywhere with Tim from Mitxela

claims.claim_text: Institutions can buy development directly: a research laboratory assigning paid staff to an open design tool accelerates its feature development in a way volunteer effort alone does not.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're putting money in to have people work on stuff
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: Projects accumulate administrative obligations that nobody signed up for, including trademarks, domain ownership and non-profit registration, which is why umbrella foundations are used; a domain held personally by an early contributor is a genuine hazard, as one project discovered when it was sold out from under them.
claims.quote_verbatim: who owns trademarks and just like even setting up, you know, 501c3s
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Grumpy Collaboration

claims.claim_text: A project can outgrow spare-time maintenance and need dedicated staff; funding that from user subscriptions rather than investors keeps the roadmap answerable to users rather than to a platform vendor's priorities.
claims.quote_verbatim: it has become so big that people cannot manage it in their spare time
claims.speaker: Keith Burzinski
claims.episode_title: Automating the Home with Keith Burzinski

claims.claim_text: Support has to be bounded explicitly: configurations expressible through the project's configuration files are supported, while users who modify the underlying source enter territory the maintainers cannot support, and their local changes break when a component is refactored.
claims.quote_verbatim: When you start hacking away at the C or C plus plus code
claims.speaker: Keith Burzinski
claims.episode_title: Automating the Home with Keith Burzinski

claims.claim_text: A practical longevity argument favours open tools even for someone who would rather pay for support: a commercial product can be discontinued, after which the user has nothing, whereas the open tool remains available.
claims.quote_verbatim: a commercial product can always be discontinued and then you're really SOL
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: The archival case is stronger still: with open tools there is no licence to expire and no vendor to lock you out, so an old virtual machine running the version that created a design can still open it decades later.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can always have an old virtual machine running key cat five
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: Every exported format is a downsampling of the design: Gerbers, mesh files and compiled binaries each discard the reasoning present in the source, which is why access to the original files matters more than access to their outputs.
claims.quote_verbatim: Every, every like output file. If you just have Gerbers is a downsampling
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Travis Goodspeed

claims.claim_text: Being free is itself an obstacle to institutional adoption: many companies will not use a tool that comes without a paid support contract, regardless of how good it becomes.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of companies simply will not switch to it because they expect to have professional paid support available
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Timing is Everything

claims.claim_text: The accountability argument runs both ways: developers distrust supplied code because a reported defect can take months to be fixed, and the answer of maintaining someone else's code oneself is unattractive, so paying for software is partly paying for an agreement that can be enforced.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't want to maintain that code
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle (2nd)

claims.claim_text: When a project hits a limit in an open component the options are to dig into unfamiliar code or to wait for someone else, and either way the schedule absorbs the delay; the same applies to a silicon defect awaiting a vendor workaround.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're reliant upon the developer of some open source software to fix it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Check The Dummy Box

claims.claim_text: The risk calculus differs by activity: using a free tool to design is a different decision from trusting a six-thousand-dollar reel of precision components to software assembled by volunteers, which is where a professional service is bought instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: would you trust, you know, reels of expensive components to a software that's been coupled together?
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Meracious Mike Manuduction

claims.claim_text: The capability of accessible tools is routinely underestimated: dense boards carrying several ball-grid-array packages, and high-speed serial designs, have been produced in them.
claims.quote_verbatim: he's using KiCad to do like USB three stuff
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: Choosing open tools deliberately to support open hardware, even when they are not the easiest option for a given job, is a consistency position that some practitioners impose on their own projects and on people working for them.
claims.quote_verbatim: I really believe in using open source software to support my open source hardware
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: Attributing a problem to a defect is unreliable while switching tools, because unfamiliarity produces the same symptom as a bug; the mirror image is that long-time users stop noticing their own tool's defects because they have been working around them for years. That applies equally to closed and open software.
claims.quote_verbatim: it could just be, I don't know where that menu is
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: Coming from a software background changes what a designer expects of a tool: the assumption that a showstopper defect can be fixed personally, or at least driven to a fix through the project's channels, is what makes the tool usable in professional work.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm accustomed to, uh, assuming that if there are any showstopper bugs in the software that I, I can fix them
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Mike Ossmann Returns! - Planetic Portalab Packaging

claims.claim_text: A schematic can only serve as the controlling document if more than one person can open it: where each seat of the tool costs thousands, only the seat holder can make a change, and a low-cost or open tool is what allows a production engineer to make and revision-control an edit at the source.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have to pay five grand for each seat of the schematic tool
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: The canonical representation of a design is its source rather than the artefacts produced from it, and treating it that way is what makes review and change control possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: we really need to look at that original source code as sort of the
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Choosing an open tool trades support for control: the user can pin a version and owns the code, but all the surrounding tooling becomes their responsibility and there is nobody to escalate to unless they pay someone.
claims.quote_verbatim: ultimately, then all the tooling's on you
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: NDA Sideshow

claims.claim_text: A business built on a free tool should accept everyone's files rather than only its own tool's output, because tying a paid service to one editor undermines the reason people came to the tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: make sure that anyone can use that service by uploading their own Gerbers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Processors, CEOs & Soldering irons - Plentiful Perfunctory Programs

claims.claim_text: The recurring commercial model proposed for open design tools is the distribution-with-support pattern taken from Linux: a packaged, regularly built version sold with support and installation services, with the changes contributed back to the upstream project.
claims.quote_verbatim: they would take Kaikad, they would develop it, they would have these regular builds
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Capacitors, Simulation and Closures - Deonerated Design Dealmaking

claims.claim_text: Large electronic design and embedded vendors, whose businesses were built on selling expensive proprietary software, began acquiring open source companies and stating publicly that the future of embedded development depends on open tools, with the revenue moving to services.
claims.quote_verbatim: We believe that the future of embedded software development depends on the wide availability of open source software and tools
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Military Electronics and The Free Eagle (Freagle) Campaign

claims.claim_text: The scale of money involved is no longer in question, given a multibillion-dollar acquisition of a company built on supporting an open kernel; the larger value, though, sits in what an open ecosystem lets other companies build rather than in what is charged for the software itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is a lot of ways to make money from, uh, open source software
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Putting a price on design blocks inside a tool is argued to be actively harmful: work that people would have given away because it is not what makes them special gets withheld and listed for sale instead, which drains the shared pool that everyone builds on.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you give people a way to monetize work that they would otherwise not believe has value, you've done a very bad thing for the world
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Opening a product's design means accepting that a competitor can take it, sell it and do it better, so the position has to be defended by staying ahead rather than by complaint.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you open it up, you've got to stay one step ahead of your competitors
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PLEASE be a die shrink

claims.claim_text: The concrete counterargument that stopped one instrument from being opened was support load: publishing the firmware invites requests about every modified variant a user creates, which the manufacturer would then be expected to answer.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'll get support requests for every tin pot thing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Re-scoping the problem

claims.claim_text: There is a line where opening code is argued against on safety grounds, such as engine management firmware, and a counter-argument that publishing it is what would let outsiders find its flaws.
claims.quote_verbatim: then other people can test for
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Re-scoping the problem

claims.claim_text: Openness and copy protection pull against each other inside a single product decision: a custom display raises the barrier to a cheap clone and lowers unit cost after tooling, while an off-the-shelf display with published firmware lets users change the fonts and behaviour but leaves nothing to stop someone reselling the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: do I try and protect that design by having custom LCD
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Your Mind Is The Tool

claims.claim_text: A server vendor publishing its code and its vulnerabilities is betting that the value lies in the delivered hardware and software rather than in secrecy, and that outside analysis of published firmware finds problems the vendor would not.
claims.quote_verbatim: The goal is to have as much stuff be public as possible
claims.speaker: Laura Abbott
claims.episode_title: Finding Hardware Flaws with Laura Abbott

claims.claim_text: Published source makes an attack cheaper rather than possible: finding the exact instruction that copied a secret into memory took reading the source, and a closed product would have yielded to the same attack after more reverse engineering.
claims.quote_verbatim: If it was closed source, you could still hack it. You would just have to take more time
claims.episode_title: New Life Skills with Joe Grand

claims.claim_text: Open projects have very poor information about who uses them and for what; poor documentation perversely improves that visibility by generating questions whose depth reveals how far a user has got, and repository watchers and stars give only a floor on the audience.
claims.quote_verbatim: usually have very, very poor data on who is using your stuff and what for
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: The productivity change over four decades is measurable in one case: a networked messaging system that took six months of C programming in the 1980s was estimated by its original author at about two and a half weeks to reconstruct today, entirely because of the open source available to build on.
claims.quote_verbatim: came back and said about two and a half weeks
claims.speaker: Lee Felsenstein
claims.episode_title: Lee Felsenstein: The Computer Revolution & Counterculture

claims.claim_text: The health of a project is readable from its contribution rate: hundreds of merge requests a week and a steady flow of first-time contributors indicate momentum, and momentum is a legitimate criterion when choosing between two projects that both technically fit.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's, I think a dozen people who make their first contribution
claims.speaker: Benjamin Cabe
claims.episode_title: Benjamin Cabé Nose Zephyr

claims.claim_text: Once vendors converge on one framework, component selection follows the software: a sensor gets chosen because it is already supported in that project's tree, which inverts the usual order of hardware and software decisions.
claims.quote_verbatim: we generally will pick a sensor because it's in the Zephyr tree
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Building Firmware and Hardware for Trade Shows with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: A project with clear commercial backing still mixes paid vendor engineering with volunteers, and the notable shift is that chip companies accustomed to controlling their whole software stack now control very little of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've always controlled everything. And now they're like, we don't get to control much of anything
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Building Firmware and Hardware for Trade Shows with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: An unopinionated control program that can be persuaded to drive almost any machine suits people building their own equipment, and the value a company can add on top of such a project is shepherding its user experience rather than replacing it.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's very unopinionated and that's really cool
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Capital equipment vendors compete on throughput figures rather than software quality because the person choosing the machine is not the person operating it; where buyer and operator are the same person, that priority inverts.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's an imbalanced priority structure
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: A tool that simply works displaces one that requires the user to submit patches and wait weeks for them to be accepted, which is why an integrated open debug probe replaced a workflow built on patching a general-purpose debug server.
claims.quote_verbatim: You don't have to every few months send another patch
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Many widely used libraries begin as something the author wrote for their own use with no expectation of an audience, published under a permissive licence on the assumption that nobody else would want it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I thought we were writing it for ourselves
claims.speaker: Piotr Esden-Tempski
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Piotr Esden-Tempski

claims.claim_text: Data under a non-disclosure agreement makes public teaching impossible: a design tool cannot have a usable tutorial if the process data needed to follow it requires signing an agreement first, which is the practical barrier open process kits remove.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you have to sign an NDA to get access to the data required to do the tutorial
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Code written with the intention that it will be read teaches, and code written only to work does not; the distinction matters when pointing a beginner at a repository, and reading code alone is not how the skill is acquired in the first place.
claims.quote_verbatim: they write their code with the intention that it is read
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pedantic or Andrantic

claims.claim_text: Adding a peripheral to an embedded Python runtime means writing the driver in C, adding the macros that expose the function to the interpreter, and rebuilding the entire firmware image, which is then loaded as a whole rather than as an add-on module.
claims.quote_verbatim: you compile that whole micro Python firmware
claims.speaker: Tony DiCola
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Tony DiCola

claims.claim_text: Acquisition of a project by a large platform company does not close it: a widely used real-time kernel bought by a cloud provider remains open, and the platform-specific additions can be stripped out by users who do not want them.
claims.quote_verbatim: But it's still like, you know, still open source
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Knob and Tube Wiring

claims.claim_text: Published source is what makes a discontinued product revivable: the development was done in the open on a public repository, and the resulting operating system is available to anyone building a device with a display, a wireless link and a phone companion application.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's all open source. So like all the develop, all the development was done on our GitHub
claims.speaker: Eric Migicovsky
claims.episode_title: Shiny New Pebble with Eric Migicovsky

claims.claim_text: Submitting a driver upstream rather than keeping it in a private package improves the code through review and puts it where the next person will look for it, at the cost of exposing it to criticism.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would encourage you to, if you've written something that hasn't been written before, to go ahead and submit it
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard's Back with Jason Kridner

claims.claim_text: The licence cost of professional design software excludes anyone without an employer to buy it, which makes capable free tools a question of access to the profession rather than a preference between tools.
claims.quote_verbatim: If I, if I didn't work at a company, I probably wouldn't be able to afford to buy it
claims.speaker: Shrouk El Attar
claims.episode_title: Creative Engineering with Shrouk El-Attar

claims.claim_text: The pattern in hardware lags software by decades rather than differing in kind: the same arguments were fought and settled in software in the 1980s and 1990s, and are being repeated now in silicon and hardware design.
claims.quote_verbatim: soft, soft, soft, soft, soft started first
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: A generated interactive bill of materials produced by an open project is a single self-contained web page, so it can be hosted behind a password and handed to a client, and later versions add trace search that turns it into a troubleshooting aid.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's just a single file. And so you just double click on it, opens in a browser
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Assembly Chat

claims.claim_text: A radio framework usable from either C++ or Python covers common tasks such as spectrum analysis and demodulation without writing code at all, which is what makes software-defined radio approachable before any programming begins.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can write code for GNU radio in either C++ or Python
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker
